## What Is an Employer of Record in Sweden


An[Employer of Record (EOR)](https://www.bolto.com/global-hr) is a third-party company that becomes the legal employer of your workers in a given country, while you retain control over their day-to-day work. In Sweden, that means the EOR handles employment contracts, payroll, taxes, and statutory benefits under Swedish law. You direct the work; the EOR holds the legal relationship.


Sweden has a well-developed labor market with strong worker protections, collective bargaining agreements, and mandatory social contributions that can be unfamiliar to foreign companies. Setting up a local entity to hire there can take months and introduce ongoing compliance obligations. An EOR sidesteps that entirely.


Instead of setting up a legal entity in Sweden, you partner with one of the[best EOR companies](https://www.bolto.com/blog/best-eor-companies-global-hiring-guide) that already has a legal presence there. Your hire works through that entity from day one, and the whole process typically takes days, not months.


### What the EOR actually handles in Sweden


Once you bring on an EOR, the legal and administrative side of employment moves to them. That covers:


- Swedish employment contracts written in accordance with local labor law, including the requirements set out under the Employment Protection Act (LAS)
- Payroll processing with correct income tax withholding and remittance to the Swedish Tax Agency (Skatteverket)
- Mandatory employer social security contributions, which run at roughly 31.42% of gross salary for most employees (Skatteverket, 2026)
- Statutory leave entitlements, including Sweden's 25-day minimum annual leave under the Annual Leave Act
- Compliance with any applicable collective bargaining agreements (CBAs), which cover a large share of the Swedish workforce


You stay focused on the work. The EOR stays accountable for the legal side.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Sweden


Sweden’s employment laws are among the most employee-protective in the world. Before you hire a single person there, you need to understand what you’re legally required to provide.


### Key Labor Laws to Know


Sweden’s employment framework rests on a few foundational laws. The[Employment Protection Act (LAS)](https://www.government.se/government-policy/labour-law-and-work-environment/) governs termination rights and notice periods. The Working Hours Act sets limits on regular and overtime hours. The Annual Leave Act guarantees workers a minimum of 25 paid vacation days per year.


Collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) are also widespread in Sweden, covering roughly[90% of workers (OECD, 2024)](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2024/10/collective-bargaining-2017-country-notes_1476607b/sweden_85921f84/28f6d8c2-en.pdf) . If your employee falls under a CBA, those terms often exceed statutory minimums and are legally binding.


### Core Compliance Requirements


- Under Sweden's Employment Protection Act (LAS), notice periods range from one to six months depending on the employee's length of service, and these periods are not waivable by the employer.
- Under Swedish law, employers are generally required to contribute to Sweden's social security system, with employer contributions running around 31.42% of gross salary (Skatteverket, 2026).
- Swedish law generally provides employees with a minimum of 25 vacation days annually, with many CBAs granting more.
- Sweden's parental leave framework provides parents with up to 480 days of state-subsidized leave per child (Forssakringskassan, 2026).


Getting any of these wrong carries real legal exposure. An EOR handles these obligations on your behalf, helping you stay compliant without requiring you to build local HR expertise from scratch. This is general information, not legal advice.

Sweden’s employer social contributions run approximately 31.42% of gross salary in 2026 (Skatteverket, 2026), covering pension, health insurance, parental leave, and unemployment. On top of that,[EOR service providers](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-service-providers) typically charge between $299 and $699 per employee per month, depending on the scope of services included.

For companies hiring a small number of people in Sweden, the EOR route is almost always the more practical option. The cost of setting up and maintaining a legal entity rarely makes sense until you have a substantial, permanent headcount in the country.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Sweden: Which Is Right for You


When you hire in Sweden, you face a foundational decision: set up a local legal entity or work with an Employer of Record (EOR). Both paths get you there, but they serve very different situations.


Setting up a Swedish entity means registering with the Swedish Companies Registration Office (Bolagsverket), opening a local bank account, and handling all employer obligations yourself. This gives you complete control and can make sense if you plan to hire a large team or build a long-term physical presence in Sweden. The downside is time. Entity setup typically takes two to three months, and ongoing administrative costs run high.


An EOR lets you hire in Sweden without owning a local entity. The EOR becomes the legal employer, handling payroll, taxes, and compliance while your new hire works for you day-to-day. If you ever need to, you can[change your employer of record](https://www.bolto.com/blog/how-to-change-employer-of-record-step-by-step) in the future.

If you are hiring one to five people in Sweden or want to move fast, an EOR is almost always the practical choice.


## FAQ


### Employer of record Sweden vs. local entity: which is faster?


An EOR in Sweden gets you up and running in days, while setting up a Swedish entity typically takes two to three months. If you’re hiring one to five people or need to move quickly, the EOR is the practical choice.


### Can I hire in Sweden without registering a company there?


Yes. An Employer of Record becomes the legal employer in Sweden on your behalf, handling employment contracts, payroll, and compliance while you maintain day-to-day management of the worker. You avoid the multi-month setup process and ongoing administrative burden of owning a Swedish subsidiary.


### What does Sweden’s 31.42% employer contribution actually cover?


Sweden’s mandatory employer social security contributions, confirmed at 31.42% for 2026 (Skatteverket, 2026), fund pension, health insurance, parental leave, unemployment insurance, and other statutory protections. This rate applies whether you hire through an EOR or operate your own Swedish entity.


### How long are notice periods when terminating an employee in Sweden?


Under Sweden’s Employment Protection Act (LAS), notice periods range from one to six months depending on how long the employee has worked for you. Under LAS, these periods are legally binding and cannot be waived, so accounting for them in workforce planning matters for cost management.


### What statutory benefits am I required to provide employees in Sweden?


Swedish employees are entitled to a minimum of 25 paid vacation days annually (Annual Leave Act, 2026) under the Annual Leave Act, extensive parental leave (up to 480 days shared between parents (Forssakringskassan, 2026)), and sick pay coverage. If your hire falls under a collective bargaining agreement, those terms often exceed these statutory minimums and are legally binding.
